procedural_history.originating_court: Commissioner under Section 263 of the IT Act
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 18.09.2017 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in ITA No.78 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Revenue preferred an appeal before the High Court challenging the order passed by the ITAT. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order passed by the ITAT.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's judgment, the Revenue filed the present appeal before the Supreme Court.

directions: The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is hereby quashed and set aside.
The order passed by the Commissioner passed in exercise of powers under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act is hereby restored.
There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Commissioner was justified in invoking the revisional jurisdiction under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, to set aside the assessment order on the grounds that it was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue.

facts: The assessee (respondent) sold a property for Rs. 33 Crores and claimed that payments made to discharge encumbrances and pay off shareholders were a "cost of improvement."
The Assessing Officer (AO) accepted this claim in the initial assessment order.
The Commissioner, using revisional jurisdiction under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act, found the AO's order to be erroneous and prejudicial to the revenue's interest and set it aside.
The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) and the High Court sided with the assessee, ruling that the Commissioner had wrongly invoked the jurisdiction under Section 263.
law: Under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act, the Commissioner can revise an order if two conditions are met: (i) the order is erroneous, and (ii) it is prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue.
Citing the case of *Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd.*, the Court affirmed that an order is prejudicial to the revenue if it results in the loss of tax that is lawfully payable.
However, if an Assessing Officer adopts one of two plausible or permissible views, the resulting order cannot be considered erroneous and prejudicial, even if it leads to a loss of revenue.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the original assessment order and the Commissioner's subsequent order.

Applying the legal principles from *Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd.*, the Court formed its own opinion that the AO's assessment order was indeed both erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue.
The Court found that the AO's erroneous order had directly resulted in a loss of tax for the Revenue.
The Court determined that this was not a case where the AO had simply chosen one of two plausible views; rather, the order itself was incorrect.
Consequently, the Court held that the Commissioner was correct to exercise the jurisdiction granted under Section 263.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the Commissioner was justified in invoking the revisional jurisdiction under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act. The Court found that the original assessment order was both erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue, thereby satisfying the twin conditions required by the law. It overturned the High Court's decision and restored the Commissioner's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amount paid by the assessee to its shareholders in settlement of litigation could be considered a 'cost of improvement' for the property sold.

facts: The assessee company sold a property named "Paville House" for Rs. 33 Crores.
There was a dispute among the company's shareholders, who were family members, which led to litigation and arbitration.
A settlement was reached via an arbitration award, requiring the company to pay three shareholders Rs. 10.35 Crores each (totaling Rs. 31.05 Crores).
This payment was for the transfer of their shares and the relinquishment of any claims to additional shares in the company.
The assessee claimed this Rs. 31.05 Crores payment as a "cost of improvement" on the property, arguing it was necessary to discharge an encumbrance to facilitate the sale.
law: Under the Income Tax Act, a "cost of improvement" is a capital expenditure that results in additions or alterations to a capital asset, thereby enhancing its value.
A payment made to remove an encumbrance that clears the title to a property can be considered a cost of improvement.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the Commissioner of Income Tax's reasoning.
It determined that the dispute was a family/shareholder issue concerning shares and control of the company, not a dispute over the title or ownership of the property itself.
The Court found that the assessee company was the clear and absolute owner of the property and there was no legal encumbrance on the property that prevented its sale.
The payment to the shareholders did not result in any additions or alterations to the property, nor did it enhance its value or give the company any new rights in the asset.
The Court concluded that the payment had "nothing to do with the improvement in the property" and was merely a settlement of shareholder claims against the company.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the assessee's claim, ruling that the amount paid to shareholders to settle a family and corporate dispute could not be considered a 'cost of improvement' for the property sold. The payment was not made to clear any title defect or encumbrance on the property itself, but rather to resolve an internal shareholder dispute.

cases.case_name: Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd. Vs. CIT
cases.principle: For the Commissioner to invoke revisional jurisdiction under Section 263(1) of the IT Act, the twin conditions of the Assessing Officer's order being (i) erroneous and (ii) prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue must both be satisfied. If one of them is absent, recourse cannot be had to the section.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If an erroneous order by an Income Tax Officer results in the Revenue losing tax that is lawfully payable, that order is prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue.
obiter: Where two views are possible and the Assessing Officer has adopted one plausible view, an order is not revisable under Section 263 even if it results in a loss of Revenue.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Applying the law laid down in Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd. (supra), the court found that the assessment order was not only erroneous but also prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue. The court held that an erroneous assessment order which results in the Revenue losing lawfully payable tax is certainly prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue. Consequently, the Commissioner was justified in exercising the jurisdiction under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act.
legal_tests_applied: To exercise jurisdiction under Section 263(1) of the Income Tax Act, the Commissioner must be satisfied of two conditions: (i) the order of the Assessing Officer sought to be revised is erroneous; and (ii) it is prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue. If one of them is absent, recourse cannot be had to Section 263(1).
An order is prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue if, due to an erroneous order of the Income Tax Officer, the Revenue is losing tax lawfully payable by a person.

An exception to the rule exists where two views are possible and the Assessing Officer has adopted one plausible view; such a decision is not revisable under Section 263, even if it has resulted in a loss of Revenue.
policy_considerations: The scheme of the Act is to levy and collect tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act and this task is entrusted to the Revenue.

The concept of 'prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue' can involve acts or orders which are subversive of the administration of revenue, such as a grievous error that might set a bad trend or pattern for similar assessments.
